facts.claim: An arbitrary wheel result of 10 versus 65 shifted median estimates of African UN membership from 25 to 45 percent.
facts.mechanism: The irrelevant number changed the starting point because people adjusted away from an anchor incompletely.
facts.commonError: Only informative or plausible starting values can anchor an estimate.
facts.whyWrong: The wheel value was random and openly irrelevant, yet estimates still separated.

facts.claim: A conjunction such as bank teller and feminist activist cannot be more probable than bank teller alone.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because adding a condition narrows the set of possible cases, so its probability cannot exceed the broader category.
facts.commonError: The more detailed option is likelier when it better matches a person's description.
facts.whyWrong: Similarity to a stereotype does not override the subset relation.

facts.claim: Recent disaster experience raises demand for hazard insurance even when the objective hazard has not risen.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because a fresh, vivid example is easier to retrieve, so availability inflates perceived frequency.
facts.commonError: Insurance demand closely tracks actuarial risk alone.
facts.whyWrong: Memory salience changes demand while the underlying hazard can remain constant.

facts.claim: Availability can make homicide seem more common than suicide even though US suicides outnumber homicides.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because homicides receive more vivid coverage, so examples come to mind more readily than the larger but quieter category.
facts.commonError: The event recalled most easily is usually the event occurring most often.
facts.whyWrong: Media salience and population frequency are different quantities.

facts.claim: Loss aversion makes a loss of a given size feel more consequential than an equal-sized gain.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because outcomes are evaluated relative to a reference point, so crossing below it carries extra psychological weight.
facts.commonError: People respond symmetrically to equal gains and losses.
facts.whyWrong: Observed willingness to trade and accept risk changes sharply between gain and loss frames.

facts.claim: Status-quo bias gives a preselected option an advantage even when switching remains possible.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because inertia, attention costs, and anticipated regret make keeping the current state easier than changing it.
facts.commonError: A default matters only when alternatives are legally blocked.
facts.whyWrong: Optional defaults change uptake without removing any alternative.

facts.claim: Describing survival as 90 of 100 alive can elicit a different response from describing mortality as 10 of 100 dead.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the positive or negative reference frame makes gains or losses salient even though the arithmetic is identical.
facts.commonError: Equivalent numbers always produce equivalent choices.
facts.whyWrong: Human evaluation responds to presentation as well as formal equivalence.

facts.claim: Unrealistic optimism can reduce preventive action when people regard themselves as less vulnerable than comparable others.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because personal risk feels exceptional, so general warnings are discounted before they motivate protection.
facts.commonError: Optimism only improves mood and has no behavioral cost.
facts.whyWrong: Underestimated personal exposure can suppress insurance, screening, or other precautions.

facts.claim: Automatic processing is fast and associative, whereas reflective processing is slower and effortful.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because routine perception and learned patterns can run without deliberate calculation, while checking and deduction consume attention.
facts.commonError: Every choice begins with a deliberate comparison of all options.
facts.whyWrong: Many judgments occur before conscious review and may never receive it.
